title: Warp and weft
hookLine: Kabir pictures the world as cloth on the Lord's loom, and the body as the place the weaver comes home

cards: Pull a thread from the hem of your sleeve and you'll find it isn't alone. Every piece of cloth is two sets of thread. One is stretched long and tight on the loom before anything begins: that's the warp.
The other runs across it, over and under, carried by the shuttle: that's the weft. Neither one is cloth by itself. Only crossed do they hold.
Kabir knew this the way a cook knows salt. And in one hymn he takes the whole loom, frame and thread and shuttle, and hangs the universe on it.

teach.b: The hymn is in Raag Asa, and it begins with a riddle. Nobody, Kabir says, knows the secret of the Weaver, who has stretched out the whole world as his warp. God here is not a king on a throne.
God is a weaver, and the world is the long thread on the frame. Then it widens.

The earth and the sky are made into the loom. The sun and the moon move across together, like the shuttles going back and forth. You can almost hear it: day, night, day, night, the weft running across the warp.
There's even a little jab in it. While you sat listening to the Vedas and the Puranas, he says, I stretched out this much of my warp. I was working, and the work was teaching me.
The weaver, Kabir sings, came to know his own home, and recognized the Lord right inside the body. The loom outside became the loom within. And it ends at the end of a life.
When the loom is broken, he says, the weaver merges thread into thread.
The cloth comes off the frame, and the thread goes back to the thread it came from. Some readers hear in this the soul returning to the One it was always part of.
Nothing in the picture is wasted, and nothing is separate: crossed, over and under, until it holds.

how: Sikhs sing and reflect on Kabir's loom hymns in kirtan and katha, reading the weaver and the cloth as pictures of the Creator, the world and the soul.

God, who stretches out the world as warp

games.q: warp and weft — tap the pairs.
p: threads stretched long on the loom

s: in this hymn, God is pictured as a king on a throne
God is the Weaver, who stretched out the whole world as his warp.
the hymn turns inward: the weaver finds the Lord inside the body
the weaver came to know his own home.
when the loom breaks, the hymn says the thread is lost
the weaver merges thread into thread.

games.q: you're Kabir, a weaver, and others sit listening to learned texts. you want to sing about God and the world. what picture do you reach for?
o: the loom you sit at every day.
games.why: the loom: earth and sky the frame, sun and moon the shuttles, the world the warp.

practice: Bring a piece of cloth close to your eyes, a sleeve, a towel, the knee of your jeans, and find the threads running one way, then the threads crossing them.

Follow one thread as far as you can before it slips under another, and notice that it never stops being itself, and never stops holding the others. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly as you trace it.

wordCard.voice: Weaver. Kabir's name for the Lord, who stretches out the whole world as warp, with the sun and moon crossing it like shuttles.

carryVoice: Your line: woven. A week that closed the sakhis and opened the bhagats, crossed and held. Seven hundred forty-nine days, and counting.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Asa, Kabir, Ang 484 (the Weaver's secret; earth and sky the loom; sun and moon; the broken loom)
